question: What is an ATC flight plan?

options.text: A clearance issued by air traffic control for the whole of a flight before the aircraft starts up
The operator's operational flight plan with the fuel figures for each leg of the planned route
A list of the navigation aids and frequencies to be used along the planned route of flight
Specified information given to air traffic services about an intended flight or part of a flight

explanation: A flight plan is specified information provided to ATS units relative to an intended flight or portion of a flight, in a set format so that it is complete and compatible with electronic data transfer.

question: Why does the flight plan have a standard format?

options.text: To ensure completeness and compatibility with electronic data transfer between units
To allow each State to add its own items without telling other States first
To fit on a single page that can be carried in a standard pilot's flight bag
To keep the amount of writing to a minimum and so reduce the pilot's workload in flight

explanation: The set format ensures that the information is complete and compatible with electronic transfer between ATS and other units. The form is printed in English and the language of the State.

question: In which language must a flight plan form be printed?

options.text: Any language chosen by the operator for its crews
The language of the State only, with no translation
English, in addition to the language of the State concerned
English and French only, in every contracting State without exception

explanation: The flight plan form should include an English text in addition to the language(s) of the State concerned.

question: What is a filed flight plan?

options.text: The flight plan as filed with an ATS unit, without any subsequent changes
The flight plan including changes brought about by subsequent clearances
The flight plan including changes cleared before the aircraft took off from departure
The flight plan as amended by the pilot after the last position report

explanation: A filed flight plan is the plan as filed by the pilot or a designated representative, without any later changes.

question: What is a current flight plan?

options.text: The flight plan as filed with an ATS unit, without any later changes at all
The flight plan for the next flight, filed while the aircraft is airborne
The most recent repetitive flight plan listing held by the ATS unit
The flight plan including changes brought about by subsequent clearances

explanation: The current flight plan includes any changes brought about by subsequent clearances.

question: What is the estimated off-block time (EOBT)?

options.text: The estimated time at which the engines will be started on the stand
The estimated time at which the aircraft will be airborne after take-off
The estimated time at which the aircraft will leave the departure FIR
The estimated time at which the aircraft will start moving for departure

explanation: EOBT is the estimated time at which the aircraft will commence movement associated with departure.

question: What is the estimated elapsed time?

options.text: The estimated time from the EOBT to the landing
The estimated time spent holding at the destination
The estimated time from engine start at the stand to engine shutdown after landing
The estimated time to proceed from one significant point to another

explanation: Estimated elapsed time is the estimated time required to proceed from one significant point to another.

question: For an IFR flight, to what point is the estimated time of arrival given?

options.text: The touchdown point on the runway in use at the destination aerodrome on arrival
The point at which the aircraft is expected to leave its cruising level
The designated point from which the instrument approach is intended to begin
The FIR boundary nearest to the destination aerodrome on the route

explanation: For IFR flights the ETA is the time over the designated point, defined by navaids, from which an instrument approach is intended to commence; if there is no navaid, over the aerodrome.

question: For a VFR flight, to what point is the estimated time of arrival given?

options.text: Over the destination aerodrome
Touchdown on the runway
The initial approach fix
The last reporting point before the aerodrome

explanation: For VFR flights the ETA is the time at which the aircraft is estimated to arrive over the aerodrome.

question: Before departure, to whom should a flight plan normally be submitted?

options.text: The ATS reporting office at the departure aerodrome
The operator's handling agent at the destination
The area control centre at the destination
The meteorological office at the departure aerodrome

explanation: A flight plan before departure is normally submitted in person or by telephone to the ATS reporting office at the departure aerodrome, or to the unit serving it if there is none.

question: A controlled flight is delayed by 30 minutes beyond its EOBT. What should be done with the flight plan?

options.text: Cancel it and fly without a flight plan
Nothing, unless the delay exceeds 3 hours beyond the EOBT
Amend it, or cancel it and submit a new one
Nothing, as ATC adjusts the times itself

explanation: After a delay of 30 minutes beyond EOBT for a controlled flight (one hour for an uncontrolled flight), the plan should be amended, or a new plan submitted and the old one cancelled.

question: After what delay must the flight plan of an uncontrolled flight be amended or replaced?

options.text: Two hours
One hour
15 minutes
30 minutes

explanation: For an uncontrolled flight with a flight plan, a delay of one hour requires the plan to be amended or replaced.

question: To whom is a flight plan filed in flight normally sent?

options.text: The station serving the ATS unit in charge of the FIR or airspace to be entered
The ATS unit at the departure aerodrome from which the aircraft took off
The operator's flight dispatch office, which then files it on the ground
The destination aerodrome's tower frequency, by a direct radio call from the aircraft

explanation: A flight plan submitted in flight is transmitted to the aeronautical station serving the ATS unit in charge of the FIR, control area, advisory area or route concerned.

question: An aircraft files a flight plan in flight to obtain ATC service. When may it proceed under the conditions requiring that service?

options.text: As soon as the flight plan has been transmitted
After waiting 10 minutes for any reply
Only after it has received an ATC clearance
Once it has passed the next reporting point

explanation: When the flight plan is to obtain ATC service, the aircraft must wait for a clearance. For an advisory service it waits for acknowledgement of receipt.

question: Which ATS unit must check and accept a flight plan?

options.text: The unit at the destination
The first ATS unit receiving it
The unit giving take-off clearance
The unit of the first FIR entered

explanation: The first ATS unit receiving a flight plan or change checks it for format, completeness and accuracy, makes it acceptable if necessary, and indicates acceptance to the originator.

question: What must the first ATS unit receiving a flight plan do with it?

options.text: Check format, completeness and accuracy, and indicate acceptance to the originator
Calculate the fuel needed and reject it if the endurance is insufficient
Pass it unchecked to the destination unit, which then checks it for errors and accepts it
Issue a clearance for the whole route and pass it to the pilot in writing

explanation: The first unit checks compliance with format and data conventions, completeness and accuracy, takes any action to make it acceptable, and indicates acceptance to the originator.

question: An operator cannot meet the RNP required for a route or area. What must it do before departure?

options.text: Cancel the flight and file again for a different route
Nothing, as RNP applies only to the oceanic areas
Advise ATC of the RNP types the aircraft is certified to meet
Add 30 minutes to the estimated elapsed time entered in item 16

explanation: An operator unable to satisfy a prescribed route or area RNP should, before departure, advise ATC of the RNP types the aircraft is certified to meet.

question: What does an RNP type such as "RNP 4" express?

options.text: Navigation accuracy within 0.4 NM of the intended position during the approach only
The need for four independent navigation systems serviceable on board the aircraft
Navigation accuracy within 4 NM of the intended position for at least 95% of flying time
Navigation accuracy within 4 NM of the intended position for the whole of the flying time

explanation: The RNP type is a containment value in NM from the intended position within which flights would be for at least 95% of the total flying time.

question: How many characters may the aircraft identification in item 7 have at most?
explanation: Item 7 is the aircraft identification, not exceeding 7 characters.

question: When is the aircraft's registration used as the item 7 identification?

options.text: Only when the operator has no three-letter designator of its own at all
Only when the flight is operated under visual flight rules in the State of registry
When its radio call sign is the registration alone, or it carries no radio
Whenever the flight is a scheduled air service for an airline operator

explanation: The registration is used when the radio call sign will be that registration alone (or preceded by the operator's telephony designator), or when the aircraft has no radio.

question: An airline flight will use the call sign made of the operator's telephony designator and a flight number. What goes in item 7?

options.text: The departure location indicator followed by the flight number
The operator's designator followed by the flight identification, e.g. ABC511
The aircraft registration followed by the flight number, e.g. DABCD511
The operator's name in full followed by the date of the flight, e.g. ABCAIR24

explanation: The operator's three-letter designator followed by the flight identification is used when the call sign will be the telephony designator plus flight identification.

question: In item 8, which letter shows a flight that will be IFR first and then change to VFR?

options.text: Z
Y
V
I

explanation: Y is IFR first and Z is VFR first; the change points are specified in item 15.

question: In item 8, which letter shows a flight that will be VFR first and then change to IFR?

options.text: Z
X
V
Y

explanation: Z is VFR first, then IFR. The point of change is given in item 15.

question: In item 8, which letter denotes a non-scheduled air transport operation?

options.text: N
G
S
X

explanation: S is scheduled air service, N non-scheduled air transport, G general aviation, M military and X other.

question: In item 8, which letter denotes general aviation?

options.text: N
G
S
X

explanation: G is general aviation; X is used for flights in none of the defined categories.

question: What does item 9 of the flight plan contain?

options.text: Number of persons on board, fuel endurance and emergency equipment carried
Number of aircraft if more than one, aircraft type and wake turbulence category
Aircraft registration, colour and markings, and the pilot in command's name
Aircraft type, communication and navigation equipment carried and the transponder modes

explanation: Item 9 has the number of aircraft (if more than one), the type designator and the wake turbulence category.

question: What is inserted in item 9 when the aircraft type has no designator?

options.text: Nothing; item 9 is left blank for such aircraft
The manufacturer's name in full, in item 9 itself
ZZZZ, with the type given in item 18 after TYP/
XXXX, with the type given in item 19 after A/

explanation: ZZZZ is inserted and the (numbers and) type(s) are specified in item 18 preceded by TYP/.

question: Which wake turbulence category applies to an aircraft with a maximum certificated take-off mass of 136 000 kg or more?

options.text: M (medium)
S (super)
H (heavy)
L (light)

explanation: H is for a maximum certificated take-off mass of 136 000 kg or more; M is between 7000 kg and 136 000 kg; L is 7000 kg or less.

question: An aircraft has a maximum certificated take-off mass of 62 800 kg. Which wake turbulence category is entered?

options.text: S
H
M
L

explanation: Between 7000 kg and 136 000 kg the category is M (medium).

question: An aircraft has a maximum certificated take-off mass of exactly 7000 kg. Which wake turbulence category is entered?

options.text: M
L
H
S

explanation: L (light) covers a maximum certificated take-off mass of 7000 kg or less.

question: In item 10, what does the letter S mean?

options.text: The aircraft carries satellite communication equipment
Standard equipment for the route is carried and serviceable
The aircraft requires special handling on this flight
The aircraft has a Mode S transponder fitted and serviceable

explanation: S means standard COM/NAV/approach aid equipment for the route is carried and serviceable; other letters show additional equipment.

question: In item 10, what does the letter N in the communication and navigation section mean?

options.text: The aircraft is fitted only with the standard equipment and nothing more
The aircraft has no transponder and must avoid all surveillance airspace
No COM/NAV/approach equipment for the route is carried, or it is unserviceable
The aircraft is fitted with a navigation system approved for the North Atlantic

explanation: N in the COM/NAV section means no COM/NAV/approach aid equipment for the route is carried, or it is unserviceable.

question: In the surveillance section of item 10, what does the letter C mean?

options.text: ADS-C capability for automatic reporting over the oceanic areas
A transponder with Mode A only, without altitude
A Mode S transponder with identification only
A transponder with Mode A (4096 codes) and Mode C

explanation: C means a transponder with Mode A (4 digits, 4096 codes) and Mode C (pressure altitude).

question: In the surveillance section of item 10, what does the letter S mean?

options.text: A transponder with Mode A only and no altitude reporting capability
A Mode S transponder with both pressure-altitude and aircraft identification
A Mode S transponder without pressure-altitude or identification transmission
Standard surveillance equipment as prescribed by the authority for the route

explanation: S means a Mode S transponder including both pressure-altitude and aircraft identification transmission.

question: In the surveillance section of item 10, what does the letter N mean?

options.text: Nil, no serviceable surveillance equipment
Mode A only, without altitude reporting
Navigation equipment carried and serviceable
Normal equipment for the route concerned

explanation: N in the surveillance section means nil.

question: In item 10, which letter shows RVSM approval?

options.text: X
R
Y
W

explanation: W shows RVSM approval and X shows approval for MNPS (North Atlantic) operations.

question: In item 10, what does the letter Z mean?

options.text: The equipment is to be notified by radio later
The aircraft is fitted for polar navigation
No equipment of any kind is carried on board the aircraft for the route
Other equipment is carried, specified in item 18

explanation: Z means other equipment is carried; it is specified in item 18 after COM/, NAV/ or DAT/ as appropriate.

question: Why is navigation capability information given in item 10?

options.text: For ATC clearance and routing purposes
For the search and rescue services only
For the operator's maintenance records
For the calculation of route charges

explanation: Information on navigation capability is provided to ATC for clearance and routing purposes.

question: What does item 13 contain for a flight plan filed before departure?

options.text: The departure location indicator and the estimated take-off time
The departure location indicator and the time of the first position report
The departure location indicator and the estimated off-block time
The destination location indicator and the total estimated elapsed time

explanation: Item 13 is the four-letter departure location indicator followed, without a space, by the EOBT.

question: The departure aerodrome has no location indicator. What is inserted in item 13?

options.text: AFIL, with the aerodrome named in item 18 after DEP/
ZZZZ, with the aerodrome named in item 18 after DEP/
The name of the aerodrome in full, in item 13 itself
XXXX, with the aerodrome named in item 19 after A/

explanation: ZZZZ is inserted and the name of the aerodrome is specified in item 18 preceded by DEP/.

question: When is "AFIL" inserted in item 13?

options.text: When the flight is an air filed military exercise
When the departure aerodrome has no location indicator
When the flight plan is filed after the EOBT at the departure has passed
When the flight plan is filed from an aircraft in flight

explanation: AFIL is used for a flight plan received from an aircraft in flight, with the time over the first point of the route instead of the EOBT.

question: For a flight plan filed in flight, what time is entered in item 13?

options.text: The time at which the flight plan was transmitted to the ATS unit
The actual or estimated time over the first point of the route it covers
The estimated time of arrival over the destination aerodrome
The estimated off-block time from the original departure aerodrome of the flight

explanation: For a flight plan received from an aircraft in flight, item 13 gives the actual or estimated time over the first point of the route to which the plan applies.

question: A flight has an EOBT of 1000 UTC and an expected take-off time of 1020 UTC. What time goes in item 13?
explanation: Item 13 takes the estimated off-block time, 1000, not the take-off time.

question: How is a true airspeed of 485 kt entered in item 15?
explanation: Knots are entered as N followed by 4 figures: N0485.

question: How is a true airspeed of 830 km/h entered in item 15?
explanation: Kilometres per hour are entered as K followed by 4 figures: K0830.

question: How is a cruising speed of Mach 0.82 entered in item 15?
explanation: Mach number to the nearest hundredth is entered as M followed by 3 figures: M082.

question: How is a cruising level of FL85 entered in item 15?
explanation: A flight level is F followed by 3 figures: F085.

question: How is a cruising altitude of 4500 ft entered in item 15?
explanation: Altitude in hundreds of feet is A followed by 3 figures: A045.

question: How is an altitude of 8400 m (in tens of metres) entered in item 15?
explanation: Altitude in tens of metres is M followed by 4 figures: M0840. A standard metric level would be S followed by 4 figures.

question: What is entered as the cruising level in item 15 for an uncontrolled VFR flight?

options.text: Nothing
VFR

explanation: For uncontrolled VFR flights the letters VFR are entered as the cruising level.

question: The departure aerodrome is not on or connected to the first ATS route. How does the item 15 route begin?

options.text: The joining point only, with no route designator
The ATS route designator, then DCT and the joining point
DCT, the joining point, then the ATS route designator
The SID designator, then DCT to the destination

explanation: If the departure aerodrome is not on or connected to the ATS route, enter DCT followed by the point of joining, followed by the route designator.

question: Between which points is DCT not needed in item 15?

options.text: Successive points both defined by geographical co-ordinates or by bearing and distance
The last point on an ATS route and a destination that is not on any route
Successive named reporting points that are not joined to each other by any ATS route
A named reporting point on an airway and a point defined by co-ordinates off it

explanation: DCT is not required between successive points defined by latitude and longitude or by bearing and distance from a navaid.

question: Which points must be entered in item 15 for a flight along ATS routes?

options.text: Only the FIR boundary points crossed by the planned route
Each point of change of speed, level, ATS route or flight rules
Only the first and last points on each ATS route of the flight, whatever changes occur
Every reporting point on the route, whether compulsory or not

explanation: Only points of change are entered: change of route, speed or level, or flight rules.

question: What change of speed must be shown as a point of change in item 15?

options.text: Any change of speed, however small it is
3% of TAS or 0.05 Mach or more
10 kt of TAS or 0.02 Mach or more
5% of TAS or 0.01 Mach or more

explanation: A change of speed of 5% TAS or 0.01 Mach or more is entered as a point of change.

question: At a point of change, only the level changes. What must be entered after the oblique stroke?

options.text: Both the cruising speed and the new cruising level
Only the new cruising level
The level, and the time at which the aircraft reaches the point
Only the cruising speed

explanation: After the point and an oblique stroke, both speed and level are entered without a space, even when only one of them changes (e.g. MAY/N0305F180).

question: What follows each point of change in item 15?

options.text: The next FIR boundary crossed after the point of change
The fuel remaining expected over the point of change
The next ATS route designator, even if unchanged, or DCT if off-route
The time at which the aircraft is expected to reach that point of change

explanation: Each point is followed by the designator of the next ATS route segment, even if the same as before, or by DCT if the next point is outside a designated route.

question: How is a point 40 NM from VOR "DUB" on a magnetic bearing of 180° entered in item 15?
explanation: The navaid identifier, then 3 figures of magnetic bearing, then 3 figures of distance: DUB180040.

question: How is the position 46°N 78°W entered in item 15, using degrees only?
explanation: Degrees only use 7 characters: 2 figures of latitude and N/S, then 3 figures of longitude and E/W: 46N078W.

question: How is the position 46°20'N 78°05'W entered in item 15, in degrees and minutes?
explanation: Degrees and minutes use 11 characters: 4 figures of latitude and N/S, then 5 figures of longitude and E/W: 4620N07805W.

question: How is a planned change from IFR to VFR at point LN shown in item 15?

options.text: VFR/LN
LN-VFR
LN VFR
LN/VFR

explanation: The point is followed by a space and VFR (or IFR for a change to IFR).

question: How is a cruise climb from 48°N 50°W at Mach 0.82 between FL290 and FL350 entered in item 15?
explanation: Cruise climb is C/, the start point, an oblique stroke, the speed, then the two levels of the layer: C/48N050W/M082F290F350.

question: How far apart should points normally be for a flight outside designated ATS routes?

options.text: Not more than 10 minutes' flying time or 100 km (54 NM)
Not more than 30 minutes' flying time or 370 km (200 NM)
At every whole degree of latitude and longitude crossed
Not more than 60 minutes' flying time or 740 km (400 NM)

explanation: Outside ATS routes, points are normally not more than 30 minutes' flying time or 370 km apart, including each change of speed, level, track or flight rules.

question: For an east-west flight between 70°N and 70°S outside ATS routes, how are the significant points normally defined?

options.text: Whole degrees of longitude at parallels of latitude spaced 5° apart
Half or whole degrees of latitude at meridians spaced 10° of longitude apart
Whole degrees of latitude at meridians spaced 20° of longitude apart
Navigation aids along the route, with no more than 200 NM between any two of them

explanation: Predominantly east-west tracks between 70°N and 70°S use half or whole degrees of latitude where they cross meridians at 10° intervals; outside those latitudes, normally 20° intervals.

question: For a north-south flight outside ATS routes, how are the significant points normally defined?

options.text: Whole degrees of latitude at meridians spaced 20° of longitude apart
Half degrees of latitude at meridians spaced 10° of longitude apart
Navigation aids along the route not more than 100 NM apart
Whole degrees of longitude at parallels of latitude spaced 5° apart

explanation: Predominantly north-south tracks use whole degrees of longitude where they cross specified parallels spaced at 5°.

question: A transition is planned between a lower and an upper ATS route oriented in the same direction. Must the transition point be entered?

options.text: Yes, with the new speed
No, it need not be inserted
Only if FL245 is crossed at that point
Yes, always with DCT

explanation: When a transition between a lower and upper ATS route is planned and the routes are oriented in the same direction, the point of transition need not be inserted.

question: What does item 16 contain?

options.text: Destination, fuel endurance and the number of persons on board
Destination and alternates only, with no times included
Destination, ETA at the destination and up to three alternate aerodromes
Destination, total estimated elapsed time and up to two alternates

explanation: Item 16 has the destination location indicator and total EET, then the location indicators of not more than two alternates.

question: A flight's trip time is 150 minutes. What is entered as the total estimated elapsed time in item 16?
explanation: Elapsed times are entered as 4 figures, hours and minutes: 150 minutes is 0230.

question: How many alternate aerodromes may be entered in item 16?

options.text: Not more than two
As many as needed
Not more than three
Not more than one

explanation: Item 16 allows the location indicators of not more than two alternate aerodromes; more can go in item 18.

question: For a flight plan filed in flight, from where is the total estimated elapsed time in item 16 measured?

options.text: From the off-block time at the departure aerodrome
From the take-off at the original departure aerodrome of the flight
From the first point of the route to which the flight plan applies
From the time at which the flight plan is transmitted

explanation: For a flight plan received from an aircraft in flight, the total EET is from the first point of the route covered by the plan.

question: In what form are all clock times entered on the flight plan?

options.text: 4 figures local time
4 figures UTC
6 figures UTC with seconds
Hours and minutes with a colon

explanation: All clock times are inserted in 4 figures UTC, and all estimated elapsed times in 4 figures (hours and minutes).

question: What is entered in item 18 if there is no other information?

options.text: Nothing
N for nil
NIL
0 (zero)

explanation: Item 18 takes 0 (zero) if there is no other information.

question: In item 18, what does the indicator EET/ give?

options.text: Significant points or FIR boundaries with the accumulated elapsed times to them
The endurance of the aircraft in hours and minutes of fuel
The estimated time at which the aircraft will leave the departure stand for the runway
The total estimated elapsed time from take-off to landing at the destination

explanation: EET/ lists significant points or FIR boundary designators with accumulated estimated elapsed times to them, when required.

question: In item 18, what does REG/ give?

options.text: The registration, if different from the item 7 identification
The region of the flight, as given in the regional supplementary procedures
The registered owner's name and address
The regulation under which the flight is operated

explanation: REG/ gives the registration markings of the aircraft, if different from the aircraft identification in item 7.

question: In item 18, what does SEL/ give?

options.text: The serial number of the plan
The SELCAL code
The selected cruising level
The selected alternate

explanation: SEL/ gives the SELCAL code, if prescribed by the ATS authority.

question: In item 18, what does OPR/ give?

options.text: The opening procedure for the departure route
The operational status of the aircraft's equipment
The operating hours of the destination aerodrome
The operator's name, if not obvious from item 7

explanation: OPR/ gives the name of the operator, if not obvious from the aircraft identification in item 7.

question: In item 18, what does STS/ give?

options.text: The standard instrument departure that the flight will use from the runway
The reason for special handling by ATS, such as STS/HOSP
The station from which the plan was transmitted
The status of the departure runway at the planned time

explanation: STS/ gives the reason for special handling by ATS, for example STS/HOSP for a hospital aircraft.

question: In item 18, what does RIF/ give?

options.text: The reason for an in-flight change of the cruising level
The route information for the return flight from the destination to departure
The route to a revised destination, followed by its location indicator
The radio frequencies to be used for each FIR on the route

explanation: RIF/ gives the route details to the revised destination aerodrome followed by its location indicator; the revised route is subject to re-clearance in flight.

question: In item 18, what does RALT/ give?

options.text: En route alternate aerodrome(s)
The radio altimeter fitted
The revised alternate in flight
The required altitude on arrival

explanation: RALT/ gives the name or indicator of en route alternate aerodrome(s). ALTN/ is used for destination alternates when ZZZZ is entered in item 16.

question: Is item 19 (supplementary information) normally transmitted in the flight plan message?

options.text: No, it is never recorded anywhere and is only for the pilot's own use
Yes, but only to the destination unit and to the first FIR unit on the route
Yes, it is transmitted to all addressees together with items 7 to 18
No, it is kept and passed only if needed, for example for search and rescue

explanation: Supplementary information is not transmitted in the FPL message. It is held available and passed only when needed, such as when the aircraft is overdue.

question: In item 19, what follows E/?

options.text: The fuel endurance in hours and minutes
The elapsed time to the destination aerodrome
The equipment carried for survival
The emergency locator frequency in use

explanation: E/ is followed by a 4-figure group giving the fuel endurance in hours and minutes.

question: A flight's trip time is 150 minutes and it carries a 30% fuel reserve on top. What is entered after E/ in item 19?
explanation: Endurance = 150 × 1.3 = 195 minutes = 3 h 15 min, entered as 0315.

question: In item 19, what is entered after P/ if the number of persons on board is not yet known?

options.text: UNK
NIL
TBN

explanation: P/ gives the total persons on board; TBN (to be notified) is used if the number is not known when filing.

question: In item 19, under R/, what is done if VHF emergency radio on 121.5 MHz is not available?

options.text: Cross out U
Cross out E
Insert V
Cross out V

explanation: Under R/, cross out U if UHF 243.0 MHz is not available, V if VHF 121.5 MHz is not available, and E if an ELT is not available.

question: In item 19, under R/, which letter is crossed out if no emergency locator transmitter is carried?

options.text: L
R
E
U

explanation: E stands for the emergency locator transmitter; it is crossed out if no ELT is available.

question: In item 19, under S/, which letter is crossed out if maritime survival equipment is not carried?

options.text: J
S
M
D

explanation: Under S/: P polar, D desert, M maritime, J jungle. Cross out each one not carried, or all of them if no survival equipment is carried.

question: In item 19, under J/ (jackets), what does crossing out F mean?

options.text: The jackets are not for flotation
The aircraft has no fire extinguisher
The life jackets have no lights
The life jackets have no fluorescein

explanation: Under J/, L is crossed out if the jackets have no lights and F if they have no fluorescein; U or V show radio capability.

question: An aircraft carries four covered yellow dinghies, each for 32 people. What is entered under D/ in item 19?

options.text: 32, 04, C not crossed out, YELLOW
04, 32, C crossed out, YELLOW COVERS
04, 128, C not crossed out, YELLOW
04, 128, C crossed out, YELLOW

explanation: D/ takes the number of dinghies (04) and total capacity (4 × 32 = 128); C is left in as they are covered, and the colour is inserted.

question: In item 19, what is entered after C/?

options.text: The company operating the flight
The name of the pilot in command
The capacity of the dinghies
The colour of the dinghy covers

explanation: C/ is followed by the name of the pilot in command. The dinghy cover indicator is the separate C within D/.

question: In item 19, what is entered after A/?

options.text: The aircraft colour and significant markings
The ATIS code letter at departure
The alternate aerodromes for the destination
The aircraft's approach category letter

explanation: A/ is followed by the colour of the aircraft and significant markings.

question: What is a repetitive flight plan (RPL)?

options.text: A plan used for training flights that return to the departure aerodrome
A plan for frequently recurring, regularly operated flights with identical basic features
A plan that is repeated by radio to each FIR along the route during the flight
A plan filed twice, once with the departure unit and once with the destination unit, for safety

explanation: An RPL relates to a series of frequently recurring, regularly operated individual flights with identical basic features, submitted by an operator for retention and repeated use by ATS units.

question: For which flights may repetitive flight plans be used?

options.text: IFR flights on the same days of consecutive weeks on at least 10 occasions, or daily for at least 10 days
VFR flights on the same days of consecutive weeks on at least 7 occasions, or daily for at least 7 days
Any scheduled flight, IFR or VFR, operated more than once a month at any time of day
IFR flights operated at least 3 times a week for a period of at least 3 months

explanation: RPLs are only for IFR flights operated regularly on the same day(s) of consecutive weeks and on at least ten occasions, or every day for at least ten consecutive days, with a high degree of stability.

question: What portion of a flight must an RPL cover?

options.text: Only the portion of the flight within the departure FIR
Only the portion along ATS routes
Only the oceanic portion of the route
The entire flight from departure to destination

explanation: RPLs shall cover the entire flight from the departure aerodrome to the destination aerodrome.

question: How long before they take effect must permanent changes to RPL listings reach the ATS agency?

options.text: At least 7 days
At least 24 hours
At least 28 days
At least 30 minutes

explanation: Amendment listings for permanent changes must reach the ATS agency at least seven days before the change becomes effective.

question: A temporary change of aircraft type on an RPL flight is needed for one day. By when must it be notified?

options.text: As early as possible and not later than 30 minutes before departure
At least 7 days before the flight, by an amendment listing
At least 3 hours before the estimated off-block time of that flight
On first radio contact with the ATS unit after take-off

explanation: Temporary changes of aircraft type and wake turbulence category, speed or cruising level are notified for each flight as early as possible and not later than 30 minutes before departure to the departure ATS reporting office.

question: Which temporary change to an RPL may be notified by radio on initial contact with the ATS unit?

options.text: A change of cruising level only
A change of the route flown
A change of destination aerodrome
A change of aircraft identification

explanation: A change of cruising level only may be notified by radio-telephony on initial contact with the ATS unit.

question: For one day, the destination of an RPL flight is changed. What must be done?

options.text: Notify the change at least 30 minutes before the planned departure
Send an amendment listing at least 7 days before the change
Cancel the RPL for that day and submit an individual flight plan
Notify the change by radio on first contact with the ATS unit

explanation: An incidental change of aircraft identification, departure aerodrome, route or destination requires the RPL to be cancelled for the day and an individual flight plan submitted.

question: An RPL flight is expected to be delayed by 30 minutes or more beyond its off-block time. What must the operator do?

options.text: Notify the ATS unit responsible for the departure aerodrome immediately
Nothing, as the RPL remains valid for the whole day concerned
Wait until the delay reaches one hour, then file a new individual flight plan
Send an amendment listing at least 7 days before the delay

explanation: The ATS unit responsible for the departure aerodrome must be notified immediately; failure may lead to automatic cancellation of the RPL for that flight.

question: What is assumed about every aircraft on an RPL listing unless otherwise noted in the remarks?

options.text: It flies VFR as a non-scheduled flight with no transponder fitted
It is a heavy aircraft with a maximum mass of 136 000 kg or more
It carries full survival equipment and dinghies for all the persons on board
It flies IFR as a scheduled flight with a 4096-code Mode A and C transponder

explanation: All RPL flights are assumed to be IFR and scheduled (type S), with 4096-code transponders with Modes A and C; anything else is noted in item Q.

question: In an RPL listing, how are days of operation shown in item K?

options.text: Sunday = 1, with X for each day of non-operation
Monday = 1, with 0 for each day of non-operation
Monday = A, with a dash for each day of non-operation
The dates of each flight written out in full

explanation: The number for each day of the week is entered in its column (Monday = 1), and 0 for each day of non-operation.

question: In an RPL listing, what is entered in item J if the last date of operation is unknown?

options.text: UFN
NIL
TBN

explanation: Item J (valid until) takes the last date of operation, or UFN (until further notice) if the duration is unknown.

question: In an RPL listing, what does a minus sign in item H indicate?

options.text: The flight plan is to be deleted from the listing
The flight has no alternate aerodrome
The flight now operates on fewer days than in the previous listing
The flight is delayed beyond its off-block time

explanation: A minus sign marks a flight plan to be deleted; a plus sign marks an initial listing or a plan not in the previous submission.

question: In what order are flight plans listed on an RPL listing?

options.text: Chronologically by EOBT only, for all aerodromes together on one list
Alphabetically by departure location indicator, then by EOBT
By destination aerodrome, then by flight number
Alphabetically by aircraft identification only

explanation: Flight plans are listed in alphabetical order of departure location indicator, and for each departure aerodrome in chronological order of EOBT.

question: How long before the EOBT should an IFR flight plan normally be filed?

options.text: At least 30 minutes
At least 60 minutes
At least 10 minutes
At least 3 hours

explanation: A flight plan should normally be filed at least 60 minutes before the EOBT. Flights subject to air traffic flow management in some regions need 3 hours.

question: A flight's EOBT is 1540 UTC and its expected take-off time is 1555 UTC. When, at the latest, should the IFR flight plan normally be filed?

options.text: 1240 UTC
1440 UTC
1510 UTC
1455 UTC

explanation: The 60-minute rule applies to the EOBT, not the take-off time: 1540 − 60 min = 1440 UTC.

question: How long before EOBT must flight plans be filed for flights subject to air traffic flow management in the European region?

options.text: At least 30 minutes
At least 1 hour
At least 24 hours
At least 3 hours

explanation: Flight plans for flights affected by ATFM measures, and in areas such as the North Atlantic, should be filed at least 3 hours before EOBT.

question: What speed is entered in item 15 of the flight plan?

options.text: The calibrated airspeed
The true airspeed
The ground speed
The indicated airspeed

explanation: Item 15 takes the true airspeed (or Mach number) for the first or whole cruising portion.

question: An aircraft will cruise at TAS 230 kt (ground speed 255 kt) at an initial pressure altitude of 15 000 ft. How does item 15 begin?
explanation: Speed is TAS in knots with 4 figures (N0230) and the pressure level is a flight level, F150, written without a space.

question: An aircraft has a maximum certificated take-off mass of 137 000 kg but will take off at 135 000 kg. Which wake turbulence category is entered?

options.text: S
H
L
M

explanation: The category depends on the maximum certificated take-off mass, not the actual mass. 137 000 kg is above 136 000 kg, so H.

question: Block fuel is 200 kg, of which 5 kg is taxi fuel, and the consumption is 60 kg/h. What endurance is entered in item 19?
explanation: Endurance is from the fuel available after taxi: 195/60 = 3.25 h = 3 h 15 min, entered as 0315.

question: In flight, by how much must the TAS or the time estimate change before ATC must be told, under the standard procedures?

options.text: TAS by 5 kt or more; the time estimate by more than 1 minute
TAS by 10 kt or more; the time estimate by more than 5 minutes
TAS by 3% or more; the time estimate by more than 5 minutes
TAS by 5% or more; the time estimate by more than 3 minutes

explanation: A variation in TAS of 5% or more, or a change of more than 3 minutes in the estimate for the next point or boundary, must be notified (some regions use 2 minutes).

question: A pilot lands at an aerodrome other than the destination in the flight plan. What must be done?

options.text: Nothing, as the flight plan is closed automatically when the aircraft lands
File a new flight plan from the aerodrome of landing to the original destination
Make sure the ATS unit at the planned destination is told within 30 minutes of the ETA there
Make sure the ATS unit at the departure aerodrome is told within 60 minutes of landing

explanation: The ATS unit at the planned destination must be informed within 30 minutes of the ETA there, otherwise search and rescue action may begin.

question: Which of these flights needs a flight plan?

options.text: Any VFR flight lasting more than 30 minutes in uncontrolled airspace
Only flights that leave the coast and fly over water
Any flight that is to receive an air traffic control service
Only flights carrying passengers for hire or reward

explanation: A flight plan is required for any flight to be provided with ATC service, IFR flights in advisory airspace, flights into designated areas or along designated routes, and flights across international borders, among others.

question: An aircraft carries maritime survival equipment only. What is done with the S/ indicators in item 19?

options.text: Cross out P, D and J
Insert M after S/
Cross out M only
Cross out S and M

explanation: Each type not carried is crossed out: polar (P), desert (D) and jungle (J) are crossed out, leaving M.
